16950:
A valedictorian is the student who graduates with the highest academic rank in their entire class. That's the heart of it. If you and 500 other students graduate from a high school or college together, and you have the best academic record among all 500 of you, you are the valedictorian of that graduating class.

The title is awarded once per graduating class. It belongs to exactly one person — the top student.
How Does Someone Become a Valedictorian?

Academic rank is almost always determined by GPA (Grade Point Average) — a number that represents the average of all a student's grades across all their courses throughout their time at that school. The student with the highest GPA at the time of graduation earns the title.

Because even a single low grade can affect the GPA, valedictorians are typically students who have worked consistently hard across every subject, every semester, for their entire time at that school — not just in one impressive final year.
The Main Duty: The Valedictory Speech

Being named valedictorian comes with an important honor and responsibility: the valedictorian traditionally delivers the farewell speech at the graduation ceremony (also called the commencement ceremony).

This speech is called the valedictory address. It is addressed to the graduating class and is meant to be a meaningful send-off — often reflecting on shared experiences, offering encouragement, and looking ahead to the future. It is usually the most prominent student speech of the entire ceremony, and it is a significant public honor to be the one giving it.
Where and When Is This Title Used?

The term is most commonly used in the United States, and it applies at both the high school and college/university level. Every graduating class — whether a small class of 30 students or a large university class of thousands — can have its own valedictorian.

The title is only relevant at the moment of graduation. It does not follow a person throughout life as an ongoing credential, but it is considered a prestigious achievement that people often mention in resumes, college applications, and biographical summaries.

You will often hear the word "valedictorian" alongside another word: salutatorian. The salutatorian is the student with the second-highest academic rank in the graduating class. The salutatorian also typically gives a speech at graduation, but it comes before the valedictorian's speech and is generally considered the secondary honor. Think of valedictorian as the gold medal and salutatorian as the silver medal.

Sometimes, two or more students finish with identical GPAs — so high that no single student stands clearly above the rest. In these cases, many schools choose to name co-valedictorians, sharing the title among all students who are tied at the top. This has become more common over time, particularly as grading practices have evolved and more students achieve perfect or near-perfect GPAs.

Some people feel co-valedictorians is a fair solution; others feel it dilutes the meaning of the title. Schools handle this differently.
A Growing Debate: Should the Title Exist at All?

In recent decades, some schools and education experts have questioned whether the valedictorian system is healthy. Their concern is that the intense competition for the top GPA can push students to make choices driven purely by grades — such as avoiding challenging courses that might lower their GPA — rather than pursuing genuine learning and intellectual curiosity.

As a result, some schools have abolished the valedictorian title entirely, choosing instead to honor all students who meet a high academic standard (a practice sometimes called "Latin honors," where graduates are recognized as cum laude, magna cum laude, or summa cum laude depending on their GPA range). Other schools have kept the tradition, seeing it as a meaningful way to recognize the highest achiever.

To remember this word simply: a valedictorian is the #1 student in a graduating class, who gives the farewell speech at graduation. Every part of the word's meaning connects to those two things — the achievement of being the best academically, and the honor of being the one who formally says goodbye to the class on everyone's behalf.
16951:
If something is valedictory, it is related to, or has the character of, a farewell — specifically a formal, intentional, and often emotionally significant goodbye that marks the end of something important.

The key idea is not just that something is last or final, but that it consciously acknowledges its own ending. It carries a sense of looking back, wrapping up, and departing with purpose.

Think about the last day of school before graduation, or a retiring athlete's final game, or a president's last speech before leaving office. There's a particular atmosphere to those moments — reflective, a little solemn, tinged with both pride and bittersweetness. That atmosphere is exactly what "valedictory" captures.

It is not just any ending. It is an ending that knows it is an ending and acknowledges that openly, often with a sense of ceremony or dignity.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Valedictory?

The adjective can describe a wide range of things, as long as they carry that farewell quality:

  • A valedictory speech — a formal farewell address, given before someone departs a role, an institution, or a stage of life. The most classic example is a graduation speech. A retiring CEO might give a valedictory address to their company.
  • A valedictory performance — a musician, actor, or athlete's final show or game, treated as a send-off. A band performing their last-ever concert could be called a valedictory performance.
  • A valedictory letter or message — a written farewell, often carrying reflection and a sense of closure. A diplomat writing a final dispatch before leaving their post might write a valedictory letter.
  • A valedictory tour — a final tour undertaken specifically to say goodbye. A retiring comedian doing a last run of shows across the country is on a valedictory tour.
  • A valedictory gesture — a final act that signals goodbye or serves as a parting statement. A leader's last major policy decision before stepping down could be called a valedictory gesture.
  • A valedictory mood or tone — even an atmosphere or feeling can be valedictory. If a novel's final chapter feels reflective, wistful, and closing, you could say it has a valedictory tone.

• "The veteran journalist wrote a valedictory column after 40 years at the newspaper, reflecting on everything she had witnessed."
  • "His valedictory speech moved the audience to tears — it felt like the closing of an era."
  • "The team's last match of the season, knowing they were losing their star player, had a valedictory quality to it."
  • "She sent a valedictory email to her colleagues on her final day at the company."
What Makes It Different From Similar Words?

This is important for precision.

  • "Final" simply means last in a sequence. A final exam is just the last exam. It has no emotional farewell quality built into it.
  • "Last" works the same way — purely positional. The last train is just the train after which no more come.
  • "Farewell" (as an adjective, e.g., "a farewell party") is the closest everyday equivalent, but it is more casual and general. "Valedictory" is more formal, more elevated, and carries a stronger suggestion of significance, reflection, and ceremony.
  • "Elegiac" means mournful or expressing grief about a loss, and while it can overlap in feeling, it leans more toward sadness about something already gone. Valedictory is about the act of departing, not purely the mourning of it.

So "valedictory" sits at the intersection of formal, farewell, and reflective. It's the word you reach for when a goodbye is significant enough to deserve acknowledgment and ceremony.

This is a formal and literary word. You will encounter it in:

  • Journalism and opinion writing ("his valedictory address to the nation")
  • Literary criticism and book reviews
  • Political writing
  • Formal speeches and essays

You would not typically use it in casual everyday conversation — it would sound oddly grand. But in writing, or in any context where a significant departure is being discussed with appropriate gravity, it is exactly the right word.
The One-Line Summary to Remember It By
Valedictory describes something that formally and meaningfully says goodbye — it belongs to the moment of departure, not just the sequence of endings.
16952: A valedictory is a farewell speech — but not just any goodbye. It is a formal, carefully prepared address delivered at an important occasion to mark the end of a significant chapter in people's lives. Think of it as the official, meaningful "last word" before a group of people move on from something they shared together.
Where You'll Most Commonly Encounter It

The word is most strongly associated with graduation ceremonies. When a school or university class graduates, one student — typically the one with the highest academic rank, called the valedictorian — stands up and speaks on behalf of the entire graduating class. That speech is the valedictory.

It is the speech that says: "We did this together. Here's what it meant. Now we go forward."

A valedictory typically does three things at once:

  1. Looks back — It reflects on the shared journey. The struggles, the growth, the memories, the people who helped along the way.
  2. Acknowledges the present moment — It marks the significance of this exact turning point, the moment of departure.
  3. Looks forward — It sends people off with encouragement, hope, or a call to go out and do something meaningful with what they've learned.

This is why a valedictory tends to feel both celebratory and bittersweet at the same time. There's joy in the achievement, but there's also the quiet ache of leaving something behind.

While graduation is the most common setting, the word can be used more broadly for any formal farewell address that carries real weight. For example:

  • A long-serving president's final speech to the nation before leaving office can be called a valedictory.
  • A retiring judge's last address to a courtroom can be a valedictory.
  • A diplomat's final statement before leaving a post can be a valedictory.
  • A celebrated writer's final published essay, if it reads like a farewell, might be called a valedictory in literary contexts.

The key in all these cases is the same: it is formal, it is final, and it carries a sense of meaningful closure.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Valedictory" is not a cold or bureaucratic word. It carries genuine emotional depth. When someone calls a speech a valedictory, they're signalling that this isn't just a routine announcement — it is a deliberate, dignified farewell that deserves to be listened to carefully. It implies that what is ending actually mattered.
How to Use It in a Sentence

• "The class president gave a heartfelt valedictory that left many in the audience in tears."
  • "The retiring general's valedictory was broadcast on national television."
  • "After forty years in the Senate, her valedictory was considered one of the most eloquent speeches the chamber had ever heard."
  • "His valedictory focused entirely on the friendships that had carried the class through four difficult years."
One Simple Way to Remember It

If you ever forget the word's meaning, anchor it to this image: a student standing at a podium, facing their graduating class for the last time, about to say goodbye on everyone's behalf. That speech — that solemn, hopeful, final address — is a valedictory. Everything else the word means flows naturally from that image.
16953: The word valet (noun) refers to someone — or something — that personally takes care of another person's needs, particularly around clothing, appearance, and convenience. It has three distinct meanings, all tied together by this idea of attentive, personal service.

This is the oldest and most traditional meaning.

A valet is a man who is employed to personally look after another man — typically a wealthy, aristocratic, or important one. He is not a general household servant who cooks or cleans the house. His job is entirely focused on his employer as a person. His duties center around:

  • Clothing: laying out the right clothes each day, brushing and pressing them, making sure everything is in perfect order.
  • Dressing: helping his employer get dressed, sometimes in formal or complicated attire.
  • Grooming: ensuring his employer looks impeccable.
  • Travel: packing and unpacking luggage, organizing everything so that his employer never has to think about such matters.
  • Personal errands: handling small but important personal tasks.

The valet is essentially a human extension of his employer's comfort and appearance. He knows his employer's wardrobe inside out, knows which cufflinks go with which shirt, and anticipates needs before they are even spoken.

This kind of valet was extremely common among the European nobility and upper classes, and you will still find the role in royal households, among certain heads of state, and among the ultra-wealthy. In literature, the most famous example is Jeeves, the impeccably efficient valet in P.G. Wodehouse's stories, who not only manages his employer Bertie Wooster's wardrobe but practically manages his entire life.

Today, outside of royalty and extreme wealth, this role has become rare. However, the most senior hotels in the world (called "butler-service" hotels) still offer this kind of personal attendant to their most important guests.

This is the most common meaning of "valet" you will encounter in everyday modern life, particularly in the phrase valet parking.

A valet here is a person employed at a hotel, restaurant, hospital, event venue, or upscale establishment whose job is to park your car for you. When you arrive, you stop at the entrance, hand your car keys to this person (the valet), and walk inside. The valet then drives your car to a parking area. When you are ready to leave, you present a ticket or give your name, and the valet retrieves your car and brings it back to the entrance for you.

The connection to Meaning 1 is clear: just as a personal valet removes the burden of managing clothes and dressing, a parking valet removes the inconvenience of finding a parking spot. It is a form of personal service — in this case, a small but convenient one.

You might hear sentences like:

  • "The restaurant offers valet service."
  • "I gave my keys to the valet."
  • "The valet brought the car around."

A valet (also called a valet stand or clothes valet) is a tall, freestanding rack or frame designed to hold a man's clothing in an organized, ready-to-wear manner.

A typical valet stand has:

  • A shaped hanger at the top (like a mini-shoulder form) for a jacket or shirt
  • A horizontal bar or clamp lower down for trousers, draped neatly
  • Sometimes a small tray at the top for cufflinks, a watch, or small accessories
  • Sometimes a shelf or rack at the bottom for shoes

The idea is simple: at the end of the day, instead of throwing your suit over a chair or hanging it haphazardly, you place it on the valet stand. It keeps your clothes wrinkle-free, organized, and ready to wear the next morning. It essentially replaces the function of a human valet when no human one is available — it "stands in" for the servant.
How the Three Meanings Fit Together

Notice the unifying thread: a valet — whether a person or an object — takes care of a man's personal appearance and comfort so that he doesn't have to do it himself. The personal manservant does it by being attentive and skilled. The parking attendant does it by handling a small but bothersome task. The furniture does it by holding your clothes ready.

The word has simply expanded over time from its original meaning into these related, service-oriented senses.

The word "valet" carries a sense of luxury, formality, and high-end service. When you hear it, it signals something above the ordinary:

  • Valet parking is more upscale than a regular parking lot.
  • A personal valet is associated with wealth and privilege.
  • A valet stand is considered a refined, old-fashioned piece of gentlemanly furniture.

The word is at home in contexts like five-star hotels, formal estates, period dramas, and premium service offerings. It is never a word you would use casually for ordinary everyday assistance.
16954: A valetudinarian is a person who is excessively and obsessively preoccupied with their own health — someone who makes their physical well-being the central, defining focus of their entire life.

Picture someone who:

  • Constantly talks about their aches, symptoms, and physical sensations — even minor ones.
  • Treats every small discomfort as a potential sign of a serious illness.
  • Avoids activities they consider even slightly risky to their health (a short walk on a cold day, eating certain foods, staying up past a certain hour).
  • Follows strict health routines, takes many precautions, and is extremely cautious about anything that could affect their body.
  • Frequently visits doctors, reads about diseases, or monitors their body with intense attention.
  • Sees themselves as fragile, delicate, or in need of special care — and expects others to acknowledge this.

This isn't someone who got sick and is temporarily worried. This is a permanent way of living and thinking — their health is their hobby, their conversation, their identity, and their daily concern.
The Crucial Nuance — Are They Actually Sick?

This is where the word gets interesting, and where many learners get confused. A valetudinarian may or may not be genuinely ill.

Case 1 — The genuinely unwell valetudinarian: Some valetudinarians do have real health problems. But instead of coping with illness and living as full a life as possible, they surrender entirely to it. Their sickness becomes their whole personality. They define themselves by their frailty, restrict their lives far beyond what their actual condition requires, and treat themselves as perpetual invalids.

Case 2 — The perfectly healthy valetudinarian: Others are not seriously sick at all, yet still behave as though they are fragile and ailing. They catastrophize minor symptoms. They live in anticipation of illness. They hover at the edge of imagined suffering.

In both cases, the label "valetudinarian" is earned not by the illness itself, but by the excessive, all-consuming relationship the person has with their own health.
How Is This Different From a Hypochondriac?

These two words are closely related, and in everyday conversation, people sometimes use them interchangeably. But there is a meaningful distinction:

  • A hypochondriac specifically fears that they have a serious disease. The core feature is anxiety about illness — they are convinced they are sick even when doctors say they are not.
  • A valetudinarian is more broadly obsessed with health and physical well-being in general — not just fear of disease, but the entire territory of bodily care, fragility, symptoms, and self-protection. A valetudinarian may know they are not seriously ill, yet still orbit their health constantly. The focus is as much on managing and protecting their body as on fearing disease.

Think of it this way: all hypochondriacs are valetudinarians, but not all valetudinarians are hypochondriacs.

"Valetudinarian" is not a neutral medical label. It carries a gently critical or mocking tone. When you call someone a valetudinarian, you are implying that their health obsession is excessive, tiresome, or self-indulgent — that they have crossed the line from reasonable self-care into something that is somewhat absurd or socially exhausting.

It's the kind of word used by someone who is quietly amused or mildly exasperated by the person in question.
A Classic Example to Make It Stick

The most famous valetudinarian in English literature is Mr. Woodhouse from Jane Austen's novel Emma. He is a wealthy, kindly old man who is utterly obsessed with health — his own and everyone else's. He worries about cold drafts, discourages people from eating rich food, frets over short carriage rides, and gently insists that everyone around him take the same precautions he does. He is not truly invalid, but he lives as though he might shatter at any moment. He is lovable, but exhausting — which is precisely the spirit the word "valetudinarian" captures.

• "My uncle is a valetudinarian who hasn't attended a single dinner party in ten years for fear of catching a cold."
  • "She had been a valetudinarian all her adult life, treating every headache as cause for alarm."
  • "The old gentleman was a confirmed valetudinarian, and no amount of reassurance from his doctor could convince him that he was not at death's door."

A valetudinarian is someone who is so absorbed in the condition of their own body — whether through fear, habit, fragility, or self-focus — that their health becomes the defining preoccupation of their life, to a degree that others find excessive.
16955:
Valiant means showing great courage and determination, especially when facing something difficult, dangerous, or overwhelming — and choosing to push forward anyway, without giving up.

It is almost always a compliment. When you call someone or something valiant, you are expressing deep admiration for the courage and effort they showed in a genuinely tough situation.

"Valiant" is not just another word for "brave." It has two layers working together:

Courage — the willingness to face something frightening or hard, without turning away.

Determined effort — the active choice to keep fighting, keep trying, and give everything you have.

Both layers need to be present. Someone who simply feels no fear isn't necessarily valiant — that's just boldness. Someone who works hard at something easy isn't valiant either. What makes something valiant is courageous effort in the face of real difficulty. The situation must be hard. The person must rise to meet it anyway.

Imagine a soldier who keeps fighting even when heavily outnumbered. Imagine a patient who endures months of painful treatment without surrendering their spirit. Imagine a small rescue team working through a storm to save someone's life. All of these can rightly be described as valiant.

The common thread: the odds were real, the difficulty was real, and they faced it with everything they had.
A Very Important Nuance — Valiant Does Not Mean Successful

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word. A valiant effort can still end in failure. In fact, "valiant" is very commonly used precisely when someone tries their absolute best but does not succeed. Saying "it was a valiant effort" means: you were courageous, you gave everything, and I deeply respect that — even though it didn't work out. The admiration is for the character shown, not the result achieved.

• It does not mean reckless or foolish. Charging blindly into danger without reason is not valiant — it is rash. Valiant carries a sense of purposefulness and dignity.
  • It does not mean ordinary, everyday bravery. Valiant is reserved for courage that is genuinely impressive and worth honoring.
  • It does not guarantee success, as explained above.
Common Collocations (Words That Often Pair With "Valiant")

These are the combinations you will most naturally encounter:

A valiant effort — a courageous and wholehearted attempt, often despite failure.
A valiant warrior / fighter / soldier — someone who fights with great bravery and determination.
A valiant struggle — a brave battle against something deeply difficult, such as illness, injustice, or loss.
A valiant hero — someone who displayed admirable, honor-worthy courage in a meaningful situation.
A valiant attempt — very similar to "valiant effort."
The Tone and Register of the Word

Valiant carries a tone of nobility and honor. It is a slightly formal, elevated word — you will find it often in literature, historical writing, speeches, news stories, and formal praise. It is not a casual, everyday word. You would not say "my friend was valiant at fixing his bike today." But in the right context — when someone truly faced something hard and rose to meet it — valiant is a powerful and precise word.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Brave is the most general word for not being afraid. Valiant goes further, adding determination, effort, and a sense of honor.

Courageous is very close to valiant, but valiant tends to emphasize the active, fighting spirit more — the sense of pressing forward against difficulty rather than simply enduring it.

Heroic is also close, but heroic often focuses on an outstanding act that helps or saves others. Valiant focuses more on the inner quality of the person — their courage and determination themselves, regardless of outcome.

Gallant is perhaps the nearest synonym, but gallant adds a layer of charm, grace, and chivalry — it is often used in a noble or romantic sense. Valiant is more straightforwardly about raw, determined courage.

Bold means willing to take risks, but lacks the sense of noble struggle and moral admiration that valiant carries.

Cowardly — retreating from fear rather than facing it.
Timid — being too afraid to act at all.
Faint-hearted — lacking the courage or resolve to push through difficulty.

If you had to capture the full meaning of valiant in one sentence, it would be this:

A valiant person faces genuine difficulty or danger with remarkable courage and unwavering determination — and is deeply admirable for doing so, whether they succeed or not.
16956: When someone does something valiantly, they do it with great courage, determination, and strength — especially when the situation is difficult, dangerous, or when they are likely to fail or suffer.

The key idea inside "valiantly" is brave effort in the face of hardship. It is not just about being brave in a calm or easy situation. It almost always appears when things are hard — when the odds are against someone, when they are tired or wounded, when failure is likely — and yet they still push forward with everything they have.

It carries a sense of admiration. When you say someone acted valiantly, you are not just describing what they did — you are quietly praising them for it. The word has a warm, respectful tone.
What kind of actions does it describe?

"Valiantly" describes how someone performs an action — not what they feel inside. It modifies a verb.

  • A soldier fights valiantly.
  • A doctor struggles valiantly to save a patient.
  • A student tries valiantly to pass a difficult exam.
  • A team competes valiantly against a far stronger opponent.

Notice that in almost every case, there is a challenge, threat, or obstacle present. The word would feel strange or even a little ironic if used in an easy, comfortable situation. You wouldn't say someone "valiantly ate their breakfast" unless you were joking.

Imagine a small army outnumbered ten to one. They know they will probably lose. They are exhausted and scared. And yet — they do not run. They stand their ground and fight with everything they have.

That is acting valiantly.

Or imagine a sick child who works hard every day in physical therapy, even though recovery is painful and slow. That child is trying valiantly to get better.

The emotion behind it is a mixture of courage + effort + dignity. The person is not giving up. They are not reckless or showing off. They are simply doing what needs to be done, without backing down, even when it costs them.

"Valiantly" is a strong, somewhat formal word. It is not something you use in casual everyday conversation very often. You are more likely to see it in:

  • Writing (stories, news reports, essays)
  • Speeches or tributes
  • Historical descriptions

In spoken conversation, people might instead say "bravely," "courageously," or "with everything they had." But in writing, "valiantly" gives a richer, more elevated feeling — a sense of nobility and honor.
A subtle but important nuance: effort is not always enough

One of the most interesting things about "valiantly" is that the person does not necessarily succeed. The word can be used even when someone fails. In fact, it is often used precisely in those moments of noble defeat.

"They fought valiantly but were eventually overwhelmed."

"She tried valiantly to save the company, but it still went bankrupt."

This is what makes the word moving. It is not a word about winners. It is a word about people who gave their best, regardless of the outcome. It honors the effort and spirit, not just the result.
Spectrum of use: big and small

While "valiantly" has heroic roots (battles, great struggles), it is used in both big and small situations in modern language:

  • Big: A firefighter who valiantly enters a burning building to rescue a child.
  • Medium: A nurse who valiantly works double shifts during a crisis to care for patients.
  • Small-but-real: A student who valiantly stays up all night to finish a project, even knowing it might not be enough.

In all three cases, the common thread is: difficult circumstances + strong effort + a sense of not giving up.

• It is not reckless bravery (like jumping off a cliff for fun). There is always a reason behind valiant effort — protecting something, achieving something, surviving something.
  • It is not quiet or hidden courage (like silently enduring pain). "Valiantly" usually involves active effort — fighting, trying, struggling, working.
  • It is not just hard work in comfortable conditions. The difficulty and the stakes matter.

Valiantly = doing something with great courage and determined effort, especially when the situation is hard, the odds are against you, or the cost is high — in a way that earns respect and admiration, regardless of whether you succeed or fail.
16957:
Valid means genuinely acceptable, well-grounded, and able to withstand scrutiny. When something is valid, it meets the required standard — it holds up when examined closely. It cannot be rightfully dismissed or ignored.

A simple way to remember it: if something is valid, it checks out. It stands on solid ground.

The opposite is invalid, meaning it fails to meet the standard — it falls apart when examined, or it has no official standing.

The word lives in two main areas of life, and once you understand both, the word will feel natural everywhere you see it.

1. Valid in Reasoning and Arguments

When someone makes a point, gives a reason, or builds an argument, it can be called valid if the reasoning is sound — meaning the conclusion genuinely follows from the evidence or premises provided, and the whole thing holds together logically.

Think of a valid argument like a well-built bridge. Every part supports the whole structure. An invalid argument is like a bridge with missing planks — it looks like it should work, but it collapses when you step on it.

"She made a valid point about the dangers of speeding." — Her point was grounded in real evidence; it was hard to argue against.

"That is a valid concern." — The worry is reasonable and based on something real, not imagined or exaggerated.

"His argument was not valid — he assumed things that weren't proven." — His reasoning had a weak foundation; it fell apart under examination.

Notice that a valid point or argument doesn't have to be one everyone agrees with. It just has to be one that is well-reasoned and cannot be easily dismissed. Someone might dislike your point but still have to admit it's valid.

2. Valid in Official and Legal Contexts

When applied to documents, licenses, tickets, contracts, or identities, valid means officially recognized, currently active, and meeting all required conditions. The key idea here is official legitimacy and whether something is still "in force."

"Is your passport still valid?" — Has it expired? Is it currently accepted for travel?

"You need a valid ID to enter." — An ID that is real, not expired, and officially recognized by the authority asking for it.

"The contract is valid for two years." — It is legally binding and in effect for two years.

"This ticket is not valid after midnight." — After midnight, the ticket loses its power; it no longer grants you entry or passage.

Think of a valid document like a key that actually opens a door. The moment it expires or is declared fake, it stops working — it becomes invalid, and the door stays shut.

There is a third, very common use of "valid" that you will hear constantly in casual speech — especially when people are talking about feelings, emotions, or personal experiences.

Here, valid means understandable, legitimate, and deserving of respect — as opposed to being silly, irrational, or something that should be brushed aside.

"Your feelings are valid." — What you feel is real and makes sense given your situation. You have every right to feel it.

"That is a valid reaction to what happened." — Given the circumstances, reacting that way is completely understandable.

This use of "valid" is essentially the speaker saying: I recognize this. I take it seriously. It is not nothing.
The Single Thread Running Through Every Use

Whether it's a logical argument, an official document, or a person's feelings — valid always carries the same core meaning:

It holds up. It meets the standard. It cannot be rightfully dismissed.

An argument is valid when its reasoning holds up. A passport is valid when it meets the official requirements. A feeling is valid when it genuinely reflects a real human experience that deserves acknowledgment.

Yes. Validity is not always all-or-nothing in everyday speech. You can qualify it:

"That is a perfectly valid excuse." — Completely valid; no question about it.

"That is a fairly valid point." — Mostly valid, perhaps with minor weaknesses.

"That is hardly a valid reason." — Barely acceptable; it almost doesn't hold up.

Certain words appear with "valid" so often that learning them together will help you recognize and use the word naturally.

A valid point is a good, solid contribution to a discussion. A valid reason is one that is genuinely accepted as sufficient. A valid concern is a worry that is understandable and grounded in reality. A valid argument is one whose logic holds together. A valid passport, valid ID, or valid license is a document that is current and officially recognized. A valid contract is one that is legally binding. A valid excuse is one that is genuinely acceptable to the person judging it.
A Final Way to Think About It

Imagine a judge — not necessarily in a court, but any kind of evaluator: a teacher grading a response, a border officer checking a passport, a friend listening to your explanation, or a philosopher picking apart an argument.

When that judge says "valid," they are saying: "This passes. This meets the standard I am applying. I accept it."

That is all "valid" ever means, no matter the context.
16958:
To validate something means to confirm that it is true, correct, legitimate, or acceptable — either by checking it against a standard, proving it with evidence, or officially approving it.

Think of it this way: when you validate something, you are essentially saying "Yes, this is real. This is correct. This counts."

The word "validate" is used in several different situations, but the same core idea runs through all of them.

1. To Prove That Something Is True or Correct

This is the most general use. When evidence, results, or experience confirm that something is accurate or sound, we say it validates that thing.

"Years of research validated the scientist's theory."

Here, the research proved the theory was correct. The theory wasn't just a guess anymore — it was confirmed.

"Her success validated his decision to invest in her business."

His decision turned out to be right. Her success was the proof.

In this sense, validate is close to confirm, prove, or support.

2. To Officially Approve or Recognize Something

Sometimes, something needs a formal stamp of approval — a signature, a seal, a mark — to be considered legal, official, or usable. That act of officially approving it is called validating it.

"Please get your parking ticket validated at the front desk."

The desk stamps or signs the ticket, making it officially recognized so you don't have to pay.

"The judge validated the contract."

The judge officially recognized it as legally binding.

"Your ticket must be validated before you board the train."

Without that approval, the ticket doesn't count.

In this sense, validate is close to authorize, certify, or officially approve.

3. To Make Someone Feel That Their Feelings or Thoughts Are Legitimate

This is a very common modern use, especially in psychology, relationships, and everyday conversation.

When you validate a person, you acknowledge that their feelings, opinions, or experiences are real, understandable, and worth taking seriously — even if you don't fully agree with them.

"When her friend listened without judging her, she felt validated."

She felt that her feelings were taken seriously. She didn't feel dismissed or told she was wrong to feel that way.

"The therapist validated the patient's anxiety by saying it made complete sense given what he had been through."

The therapist wasn't saying the patient was right or wrong — she was saying: "Your reaction is understandable. It is real. It matters."

"He just wanted someone to validate his frustration, not fix it."

He didn't need a solution. He needed someone to acknowledge that his frustration was legitimate.

This use is important. Validating someone's feelings is not the same as agreeing with them. It simply means you recognize that what they feel is real and makes sense from their point of view.

4. To Check That Something Meets Required Standards (Technical Use)

In technology, systems, and processes, to validate means to verify that something meets the required rules or format before it is accepted.

"The website validates your email address to make sure it is in the correct format."

It checks that your email has an "@" sign, a domain name, etc. If it doesn't fit the required format, it won't be accepted.

"The system validated the user's identity before granting access."

It checked that the user was who they claimed to be.

"Researchers need to validate a new test before using it on patients."

They must verify that the test actually measures what it is supposed to measure, reliably and accurately.

The opposite of validate is invalidate — to prove something is false, void it officially, or reject something as incorrect or unacceptable.

"New evidence invalidated the old theory."
"The unsigned form was invalidated by the court."

FormExample
Validation (noun)"She sought validation from her peers."
Valid (adjective)"That is a valid argument."
Invalid (adjective)"The ticket was invalid after midnight."
Validating (present participle)"He was validating the results."
Validated (past tense)"The data has been validated."

Imagine a rubber stamp. When you stamp something, you are saying: "This is approved. This is real. This passes." That stamp — whether it is emotional acknowledgment, official approval, or scientific proof — is the act of validating.

The question "validate" always answers is:

"Does this truly count?" — and when you validate something, the answer is yes.
16959: A valise is a small bag used for carrying personal belongings — clothes, toiletries, and other essentials — when you travel. Think of it as a compact, hand-held travel bag, somewhere between a handbag and a small suitcase.

A valise is typically:

  • Small to medium in size — large enough to hold a change of clothes and a few personal items, but not big enough to pack for a long vacation
  • Rectangular or slightly rounded in shape, like a small suitcase
  • Carried by a handle on top, in your hand
  • Soft-sided, traditionally made of leather or sturdy fabric

A valise is meant for short trips — a night or two away from home. It holds just the basics: some clothes, toiletries, maybe a book. It's not meant for long journeys with a lot of luggage. Because of its compact size, it's easy to carry around, slip under a seat on a train, or take into a hotel room without hassle.
The feel and tone of the word

"Valise" is an older, somewhat formal or literary word. You're more likely to encounter it in classic novels, period films, or formal writing than in everyday modern conversation. If someone today said, "I packed my valise for the trip," it would sound slightly old-fashioned or elegant.

In modern everyday speech, people tend to use words like overnight bag, carry-on bag, travel bag, or just small suitcase instead. But "valise" is still understood and occasionally used, especially in writing.

• She arrived at the inn with only a small leather valise.
  • He threw a few shirts into his valise and caught the morning train.
  • The detective set his valise on the table and began unpacking his tools.
  • A valise sat by the door, packed and ready for her early departure.
A valise is a small, hand-carried travel bag used to pack personal items for a short trip — essentially a compact, old-fashioned version of what we'd today call an overnight bag.
